newsitem.title: FRANCE: Criminal Sobhraj lands in France from India.
newsitem.headline: Criminal Sobhraj lands in France from India.

text.p: Notorious criminal Charles Sobhraj arrived in Paris on Tuesday after being released from 20 years in Indian prisons and was immediately taken away to French police headquarters.
Police sources said he was escorted away by police in Paris after landing at 6.40 (0440 GMT) aboard Air France flight 147 at Paris's Charles de Gaulle from Delhi.
The sources said Sobhraj, who claims French citizenship, was to be notified of an unspecified judicial document.
His lawyer Jacques Verges, saying his client was legally a free man, angrily left the airport without seeing him.
"Sobhraj is being held somewhere. I am convinced they will have to release him," Verges told reporters. He suspected police were trying to prevent Sobhraj from talking to the press.
Sobhraj, who was born to an Indian father and Vietnamese mother, served 20 years in prison in India on a string of charges including murder and robbery committed across Asia.
Verges said whatever Sobhraj may have done was covered by the French statute of limitations which bans prosecution after 10 years.
"If the law is applied, there is no legal basis to prosecute him in France, whether some people like it or not," he said.
"Detention would be a breach of his freedom, an offence which I will oppose," he said.
Sobhraj was first arrested in India for holding up a hotel jewellery shop in 1971. He was later charged with a long string of crimes, serving time for some and winning acquittal in others.

India ordered him deported in February but France refused to accept him pending checks on his past record and nationality claim. Paris eventually agreed on Monday that he had a strong and legitimate claim for French citizenship.
French Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux said Sobhraj would have to apply for a certificate of citizenship from a judge, but indicated it would be a formality.
"We have very strong reasons to believe that his nationality is French," Doutriaux said.

Two officials of India's Foreigners' Regional Registration Office (FRRO) accompanied Sobhraj to Paris to hand him over to the French authorities. Police said he would be questioned on his legal situation.

Sobhraj plans to concentrate on working on a $15 million English-language film based on his life, to be produced in France with American actors. He has said he would write the script but would not play the title role.
Sobhraj, whose criminal exploits have been the subject of two books, was philosophical as he left Delhi. "I have no choice," he said.
Wearing a dark blue blazer and grey trousers, he told reporters in Delhi that he was optimistic about his return to India where he has two half-sisters.
"I will definitely come back," he said.
He had said that once set free he would like to roam the streets of Paris to enjoy his freedom. "I want to take a walk on the bank of the River Seine in Paris," he said.
